title: FRM Liquidity, Lesson 5: Repo and secured funding - why the safest source disappears first
subtitle: Funding against collateral sounds safe, right up until haircuts rise and the whole market has to sell at once
whyItMatters: Repo is the bloodstream of short-term funding for financial institutions, and it is where the 2008 crisis actually began - not in retail deposits but in the wholesale funding market. The mechanism that broke it is a feedback loop in which every participant behaves rationally.
openingQuestion: In a repo transaction the haircut rises from 2% to 10%. Against the same collateral, how much less can the borrower raise?
openingOptions: About 8% of the value of the assets, which has to be funded from elsewhere
Nothing changes, since the haircut only affects the repo rate
About 10% of the value of the assets, matching the new haircut exactly
It cannot be determined without knowing the term of the repo contract
explanation: The haircut is the part of the asset value that does not count towards the loan: a 2% haircut means 100 of collateral raises 98, while a 10% haircut raises only 90. The 8 of difference has to be replaced from another source or by selling assets. What makes it dangerous is that haircuts rise for everyone at the same time when markets tighten, so everyone has to sell the same asset on the same day - and that selling drives the price down, which pushes haircuts higher still.

diagram.label: Markets tighten and collateral prices become more volatile
Lenders raise haircuts to protect themselves
Borrowers can raise less and sell assets to cover the shortfall
Selling together drives prices down and haircuts rise again - the loop closes

realWorldExample.description: Many institutions funded long-dated assets with overnight repo, rolling the contract every single day. When haircuts on structured collateral jumped and some lenders stopped accepting that collateral altogether, the funding did not taper off - it vanished within days. The balance sheet had not changed at all, but the ability to keep financing it was gone.

quiz.question: Scenario: collateral worth 100bn with a 5% haircut. How much can the borrower raise?
options: 100bn (= the full market value of the collateral posted)
105bn (= 100 × 1.05, adding the haircut onto the loan)
95bn (= 100 × 0.95, with the haircut already deducted)
5bn (= the haircut portion of the collateral value)
quiz.explanation: The haircut is the cushion the lender keeps back against a price fall before it can liquidate: 100 × (1 − 0.05) = 95bn. It protects the lender and it is also the channel through which market conditions feed straight into the borrower's funding capacity.

quiz.question: Why is using overnight repo to fund long-dated assets dangerous?
options: Because overnight repo does not permit the collateral to be substituted
Because the overnight repo rate is always above the term repo rate
Because long-dated assets are not accepted as repo collateral at all
Because the risk sits in having to roll the contract every single day
quiz.explanation: This is maturity mismatch in its most extreme form: the asset runs for years while the funding lives one night. As long as the roll keeps happening everything looks smooth, but on the day it does not, the entire amount has to be repaid at once. Substitution is normally permitted in repo documentation, long-dated bonds are among the most commonly pledged collateral there is, and overnight funding is usually the cheapest leg of the curve - which is precisely what makes the arrangement so tempting.

quiz.question: What is the feedback loop that makes a repo market crisis self-amplifying?
options: Higher haircuts force selling, selling drives prices down, haircuts rise again
Higher repo rates push borrowers to switch towards retail deposit funding
Tighter regulation reduces the number of participants active in the market
Lenders demand higher-quality collateral so the cost of funding increases
quiz.explanation: Every step in the loop is rational for whoever takes it: the lender raises the haircut to protect itself, the borrower sells assets to cover the shortfall. Added together they produce exactly the outcome each side was guarding against, and the loop runs on a timescale of days rather than months. The other options describe real effects, but none of them feeds back on itself - a shift to deposits or a change in collateral standards raises costs without making the next round worse.

quiz.question: Why can secured funding disappear faster than retail deposits?
options: Because the collateral has to be revalued on a monthly cycle
Because the counterparty is an institution with no deposit insurance
Because repo always carries a longer term than a demand deposit
Because individual customers follow the news faster than institutions do
quiz.explanation: Retail depositors are insured up to a cap and generally react slowly. A repo counterparty is an institution that watches closely, has no insurance at all, and can simply decline to roll the contract the following morning - it does not need to withdraw anything, only to stop. Repo is usually much shorter-dated than a deposit book rather than longer, and revaluation happens daily under standard documentation, so neither of those is what drives the speed.

quiz.question: Which measure reduces repo funding risk most durably?
options: Moving all of the repo business to one single large counterparty
Holding more collateral so that a larger amount can be borrowed against
Lengthening funding and spreading the maturities instead of concentrating overnight
Negotiating a fixed haircut that does not move with market conditions
quiz.explanation: The exposure here is rollover risk, so the durable cure is to reduce how much has to be rolled on any given day. Holding more collateral does not help when haircuts rise across every asset class at once, and concentrating with one counterparty simply swaps market risk for concentration risk. A contractually fixed haircut sounds attractive but is priced accordingly and is the first term a lender walks away from in a crisis - the counterparty declines to renew rather than breaching the term.

practicePrompt.question: A bank funds 100,000bn of bonds through repo at a 2% haircut. Markets tighten and the haircut is raised to 8%. How much extra cash does the bank need?
options: 6,000bn (= 8% − 2% applied to 100,000bn of collateral)
8,000bn (= 8% of the 100,000bn of assets pledged)
2,000bn (= the original 2% haircut level)
10,000bn (= 8% plus 2%, the two levels added together)
practicePrompt.explanation: At a 2% haircut, 100,000bn of bonds raises 98,000bn and the bank funds 2,000bn itself. At 8%, the same bonds raise only 92,000bn, so the amount it has to fund itself rises to 8,000bn - meaning it needs another 6,000bn in cash without having bought a single new asset. This is the amplifier: the cheapest way to find 6,000bn is to sell some of the bonds, that selling pushes prices down, lower prices justify a higher haircut still, and the loop feeds itself. Nobody defaulted, nobody withdrew, and the funding evaporated anyway.

keyTakeaways: The haircut decides how much a given pool of collateral raises: 100 at a 5% haircut gives 95
Overnight repo against long-dated assets is extreme maturity mismatch - the risk is the daily roll
Higher haircuts, forced selling, falling prices, higher haircuts again is a self-amplifying loop
Wholesale funding disappears faster than retail deposits because the counterparty need not withdraw, only decline to roll

summary.keyIdea: Secured funding is safer for the lender, not for the borrower. For the borrower it adds one more channel through which market conditions feed straight into whether the firm survives.

application.message: When you read an institution's funding profile, look at the share of short-term wholesale funding and at how concentrated the maturity dates are. Those two figures say more about survival than the total stock of liquid assets it holds.

sections.text: Borrowing against collateral sounds safer than borrowing unsecured. For the lender it is. For the borrower, it opens one more route for the market to tighten its grip.
The haircut: the transmission channel few people watch

The haircut decides how much cash a pool of assets raises. In calm markets it is small and stable, so nobody pays attention to it. When volatility rises, lenders raise it to protect themselves - entirely reasonably - and the borrower's funding capacity drops immediately without a single line of the balance sheet changing.
The risk is having to roll, not having to repay

Funding a multi-year asset with overnight repo means finding the entire amount again every morning. This runs smoothly for thousands of consecutive days, which creates the impression of a stable source. It is not stable - it simply has not yet met the day on which nobody wants to lend.
A loop in which every step is rational

Haircuts rise, the borrower is short of cash and sells assets, many borrowers sell the same asset and the price falls, the falling price raises volatility, and higher volatility pushes haircuts up again. Nobody in the chain has acted irrationally, and that is precisely what makes the loop so hard to stop from the inside.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: A repo counterparty does not need to withdraw its money to bring you down. It only needs to decline to roll the contract the following morning.
The haircut rises two points and half the portfolio has to go

A fund holds 100 of bonds funded by repo at a 2% haircut. The counterparty lends 98 and the fund puts up 2 of its own capital - fifty times leverage. Markets get volatile and the counterparty raises the haircut to 4%. The same portfolio now raises only 96, and 2 of capital supports 2 / 0.04 = 50 of assets. The fund has to inject more capital or sell 50 out of 100 - half the book, in a single morning, not because anyone asked for their money back but because one parameter moved from 2 to 4.

sections.label: What makes it a systemic problem
sections.text: The haircut does not rise for one fund alone. It rises for every borrower against that asset class, at the same moment, because every counterparty is looking at the same volatility reading. So a lot of funds have to sell the same thing on the same morning. Prices fall, volatility rises further, counterparties raise haircuts again - and the loop runs on without a single step in it being anyone's misconduct. Each lender is protecting itself in an entirely reasonable way.

lines: Leverage in repo is not a number you choose; it is the reciprocal of a parameter somebody else chooses.
And they change it at exactly the moment you have the least room to manoeuvre.
